name: Genetics acceptance / shave clean

angle.text: Men with limited beard growth, or who prefer their face without one, shave clean for a neat look and open view of the jaw. Looksmax forum threads weigh clean-shaven against stubble, and studies of preferences show results that depend on context.

summary: The shave-it-off school of style: accept limited beard growth and go clean; preferences in studies depend on context.
note: Based on opinion and photo-rating threads; attractiveness studies show context-dependent preferences.
currentQuick:
Genetics acceptance is the idea that men who grow sparse or patchy facial hair should shave clean rather than keep a beard. It is argued in forum threads comparing clean-shaven and stubbled looks.
Research on beards and attractiveness finds preferences that vary with context, such as how common beards are and what the rater is looking for, rather than a single best choice.
How it works: Beard growth depends mainly on dihydrotestosterone and genetics. The practice itself is simply shaving and presenting a clean face.
Risks and caveats: Shaving is low-risk; one forum poster reports it irritates acne-prone skin. Studies of respirator fit note that clean-shaven faces fit respirators better than bearded ones, though only 47 percent of clean-shaven men achieved adequate fit in one study.
deepLead:
Genetics acceptance, or shaving clean, is a looksmaxxing style position that men who cannot grow a full beard, or who look better without one in their own judgment, should shave rather than keep patchy or sparse facial hair. It sits within style metas, discussed on forums such as looksmax.org in threads weighing clean-shaven faces against stubble or beards.
Beard growth begins at puberty, is driven by dihydrotestosterone, and varies partly by genetics. Studies of attractiveness find that preferences for beardedness depend on context, including how common beards are and the rater's mating strategy, rather than pointing to a single best option.

name: Castor oil lashes

angle.text: Users brush castor oil along the lash line in the belief it lengthens or thickens lashes, a habit common in social media beauty content and looksmaxxing talk on lashes and brows. No trial showing it grows lashes was found.

summary: Folk habit of oiling the lash line for longer lashes; popular online, with no trial showing it grows lashes.
note: Non-sterile oil should not get in the eyes; rare contact allergy.
currentQuick:
Castor oil is brushed on the lashes by people hoping for length and thickness. It is cheap and widely promoted on social media.
No clinical trial has shown it increases lash growth. Sources say any visible effect would more likely be a glossier, conditioned look, and the only product approved for lash growth in the sources is bimatoprost.
How it works: Proponents credit moisture and improved follicle circulation. No mechanism for lash growth has been demonstrated; related work on ricinoleic acid concerns scalp hair loss.
Risks and caveats: Generally low-risk topically, with rare contact dermatitis reported. Summaries note that non-sterile castor oil in the eyes can cause irritation, infection or corneal damage.
deepLead:
Castor oil on eyelashes is a folk practice in which castor oil, pressed from Ricinus communis seeds, is brushed along the lash line in the belief that it lengthens or thickens lashes. It is common in social media beauty content and in looksmaxxing discussion of lashes and brows.
A general reference work on castor oil states that no high-quality clinical trials show it stimulates eyelash growth, and that thickening claims rest on user reports. The only prescription product approved for eyelash growth named in the sources is bimatoprost (Latisse).

name: Lash growth serum (peptide)

angle.text: Users apply over-the-counter peptide serums to make lashes look longer and fuller, as a non-prescription alternative to prostaglandin products. Trials of the peptide versions were not found.

summary: Cosmetic peptide serums sold for fuller lashes; popular, but no trials of the peptide versions were found.
note: Distinct from prescription bimatoprost (Latisse), the approved product.
currentQuick:
Lash serums are cosmetic liquids brushed along the upper lash line. Some use peptides rather than the prostaglandin drug found in Latisse.
The sources reviewed include trial-level information only for bimatoprost. No published human studies of peptide serums were found.
How it works: Brands claim peptides condition or support lashes. Bimatoprost, by contrast, is a prostaglandin analogue; peptide products avoid it, reportedly in part due to regulation in Canada and California.
Risks and caveats: Peptide serums are sold as cosmetics. For bimatoprost, reported effects include infection from reused applicators and eyelid darkening.
deepLead:
Peptide lash growth serums are over-the-counter cosmetic products applied to the lash line to make lashes look longer or fuller. Some brands use peptides instead of prostaglandin analogues, and a reference work links this to regulatory rules in Canada and California.
The best-documented lash-growth product is bimatoprost (Latisse), a prescription prostaglandin analogue; its manufacturer reports visible growth within 16 weeks and up to about 25 percent more length. The sources reviewed contain no published human trials of peptide serums.

name: Microblading

angle.text: Men and women get microblading to have thicker, darker or more symmetrical brows that last roughly a couple of years. The fuller brow is visible straight after the procedure; the literature on it is mostly case reports of complications.

summary: Hand-drawn brow tattoo for fuller-looking brows; lasts roughly a couple of years, with a case-report literature of complications.
note: A tattoo: allergic and granulomatous reactions, infection and fading are documented.
currentQuick:
Microblading is a semi-permanent tattoo in which a technician draws fine hair-like strokes of pigment into the brow skin. It is used for sparse or uneven brows and has been discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a route to thicker, darker brows.
Results are reported to last up to about two years with touch-ups. The research base is mostly reviews and case reports, and members of the forums disagree about how natural it looks on men.
How it works: A handheld blade deposits pigment, often iron-oxide based, into the superficial dermis. Fading is gradual and depends on pigment, sun exposure and skin type.
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include allergic reactions, granulomatous reactions, infection and pigment migration. Removal can require laser treatment. In the US there is no federal standard for ink testing.
deepLead:
Microblading is a semi-permanent cosmetic tattooing technique for eyebrows in which a technician uses a handheld tool with fine blades or needles to draw hair-like strokes of pigment into the upper dermis, intended to make brows look fuller, darker or more symmetrical. A dermatology review describes it as a form of superficial micropigmentation that deposits pigment as deep as the papillary dermis.
Wikipedia reports that the technique was popular in Singapore by about 2007 and in the US and Canada by the mid-2010s, and results are said to last up to about two years, with touch-ups recommended around six weeks and then every 12 to 18 months. Published literature consists largely of reviews and case reports of complications, including allergic reactions, granulomatous reactions and infections. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to get darker, thicker brows, alongside alternatives such as minoxidil.

name: Brow microshading / powder brows

angle.text: Users choose microshading or powder brows for a soft, filled-in finish rather than hair-like strokes. The result is visible right away and fades over time; little published research exists on it specifically.

summary: Tattooed, soft-shaded brow fill that fades over time; closely related to microblading, with little published research of its own.
note: A tattoo: pigment reactions, infection and difficult removal are documented.
currentQuick:
Microshading or powder brows is a cosmetic tattoo that fills the brows with a soft, makeup-like gradient instead of drawn hairs. It is offered at tattoo and beauty studios.
The sources reviewed describe brow tattooing generally rather than this technique specifically, so published evidence on it by name is thin.
How it works: A technician deposits pigment, commonly iron-oxide based, into the skin to create a shaded brow shape. Results fade gradually and touch-ups are typically recommended.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include allergic reactions, infection, granulomas, keloids and pigment migration, and removal can be hard. Regulation varies; in the US there is no federal technician standard.
deepLead:
Brow microshading, also marketed as powder brows or ombre brows, is a form of cosmetic eyebrow tattooing intended to give a soft, filled-in, makeup-like finish rather than individual hair-like strokes. It belongs to the wider field of permanent makeup, in which pigment is deposited in the dermis.
The sources reviewed for this article describe eyebrow tattooing in general but do not describe microshading or powder brows by name. Reference works report that cosmetic brow tattoos fade over time, can usually be removed only with difficulty, and carry risks including allergic reactions, infection, granulomas and pigment migration.

name: Brow henna

angle.text: Users get brow henna in salons or with at-home kits to tint sparse or light brows, which look darker and fuller for days to weeks. The stain is visible immediately.

summary: A plant-based semi-permanent stain for brows that lasts days to weeks; the main documented risk is adulterated 'black henna' products containing PPD.
note: Black henna products may contain PPD, linked to severe allergic reactions; FDA has not approved henna for skin.
currentQuick:
Brow henna is a paste made from powdered henna leaves that stains brow hairs and the skin underneath, making brows look darker and more filled in. It is done in salons or with at-home kits.
The colour is temporary, with the skin stain generally fading over one to three weeks. No clinical studies specific to eyebrow henna were found.
How it works: The lawsone dye in henna binds to the keratin in hair and the outer skin layer, producing an orange-to-reddish-brown stain that darkens over a few days.
Risks and caveats: Natural henna is regarded differently from products sold as black henna, which often contain PPD and have been linked to severe allergic reactions and scarring. The US FDA has not approved henna for direct skin application.
deepLead:
Brow henna, also called henna brows, is a semi-permanent way of tinting eyebrow hair and the skin beneath it using a paste made from the powdered leaves of the henna plant. It is offered mainly by brow salons and is also sold as an at-home kit, and it is used to make sparse or light brows look darker and fuller.
Henna has a long history as a dye for hair, skin and nails, originating in North Africa and the Middle East. Wikipedia notes that its use as a temporary substitute for eyebrow pencil is comparatively recent. The stain sits on the outer layer of skin and fades over roughly one to three weeks, with the skin stain usually fading sooner than the colour on hair.
No clinical studies of henna specifically for eyebrows were found. Regulators distinguish natural henna from so-called black henna, which often contains para-phenylenediamine (PPD) and has been linked to severe allergic reactions; the US FDA has not approved henna for direct application to skin.

name: Mascara / waterproof mascara

angle.text: Mascara is applied to darken, thicken, lengthen and define lashes, with waterproof versions staying put through water and sweat. The change is visible as soon as it is applied; research testing its effect on perceived looks was not found.

summary: A lash-darkening cosmetic with a long history; waterproof versions resist water and are harder to remove, and no research tests its looks effect.
note: Waterproof types ranked highest for detected organic fluorine (PFAS indicator) in a 2021 cosmetics survey.
currentQuick:
Mascara darkens, thickens and lengthens eyelashes using pigments, oils and waxes. Waterproof versions resist water and sweat and typically need an oil-based remover.
Some men in looksmaxxing forums discuss using it on the lower lashes for a more defined eye area. No clinical studies of its effect on attractiveness were found.
How it works: A pigmented coating on the lash hairs makes them look darker, thicker and longer; the effect is temporary and wears off or is washed away.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include allergic reactions, eyelid swelling, styes and microbial contamination of old product. A 2021 study found organic fluorine, a PFAS marker, most often in waterproof mascara.
deepLead:
Mascara is a cosmetic applied to the eyelashes to darken, thicken, lengthen and define them. It is most commonly a liquid in a tube with a brush applicator, and formulas are built from pigments, oils, waxes and preservatives. Waterproof versions use hydrophobic ingredients so they resist water and sweat.
Eye darkening with kohl dates to about 4000 BC in ancient Egypt, and commercial mascara developed from the 19th-century work of Eugene Rimmel and the early 20th-century Maybelline business. In looksmaxxing communities, some male users discuss mascara as a way to make the eye area look more defined, usually with concern about being noticed.
Reported risks include allergic reactions, styes and eyelid swelling; waterproof products had the highest rate of detected organic fluorine, an indicator of PFAS, in a 2021 survey of cosmetics. No clinical trials of mascara as a looks intervention were found.

name: Individual false lashes / magnetic lashes

chain: Artificial lashes attach to lash line
angle.text: Users add strip, individual or magnetic lashes for instant length and volume. The look is visible right away and temporary; no clinical research on the products was found.

summary: Glue-on or magnet-on artificial lashes for instant length and volume; the look is temporary and no clinical research exists.
note: Magnets may be a hazard in MRI rooms; adhesives can cause reactions.
currentQuick:
Individual false lashes are applied one by one by a technician and last a few weeks, while magnetic lashes clip on with small magnets and are removed daily. Both add apparent length and density.
No clinical studies of either were found.
How it works: Synthetic lashes are attached to or clamped around natural lashes, adding visible length and volume without changing the natural lash.
Risks and caveats: Adhesives used for glued lashes can cause skin sensitivity in some people, and magnetic lashes may pose a hazard near MRI machines.
deepLead:
False eyelashes are artificial lashes attached to or near the natural lash line to add length, volume or density. Common forms are strip lashes, individual lash extensions applied one at a time by a technician, and magnetic lashes that clamp onto the natural lashes without glue.
Artificial lashes date back more than a century: a 1902-1903 British patent by Karl Nessler and a 1911 US patent by Anna Taylor are recorded, and magnetic lashes were invented in 2014 by Katy Stoka as a glue-free alternative. No clinical studies of individual or magnetic lashes were found.

name: Brow soap / brow styling soap

angle.text: Users brush brow styling soap through their eyebrows to hold hairs up for the fluffy, laminated look popular in recent beauty trends. The fuller brow shows immediately; no published research exists.

summary: A styling soap that sets brow hairs upward for a fluffy look; a cosmetic with no published research behind it.
note: No studies found; effect lasts until the product is washed off.
currentQuick:
Brow soap is a styling product brushed through eyebrow hairs to hold them up and out for a fuller, fluffier look. It is part of the broader family of brow gels and cosmetics.
No clinical studies or detailed reference material on brow soap were found.
How it works: The product coats the brow hairs and holds them in position until it is removed.
Risks and caveats: No product-specific safety data were found. As with other periocular cosmetics, skin sensitivity reactions are a general consideration.
deepLead:
Brow soap, or brow styling soap, is a waxy or gel-like soap product brushed through eyebrow hairs to hold them upward and brushed out, producing the 'fluffy' or 'laminated' brow look popular in recent beauty trends. It falls in the same functional category as brow gels, which Wikipedia describes as cosmetics that add texture and hold to brows.
Little published material exists on the category. No clinical studies of brow soap were found, and the sources loaded for this article do not cover soap-based brow products specifically.

name: Brow shaping guide / stencil

angle.text: Users place a stencil over the brow to outline a target shape, then fill in with pencil or powder or trim to its edge for neater, more symmetrical brows. The shape is visible right away; no research exists on the tool.

summary: A template that outlines a brow shape for filling or trimming; no research exists on it.
note: No studies found; hair removal done with it carries the usual risks of the chosen method.
currentQuick:
A brow stencil is a plastic or similar template laid over the brow to mark a shape. Users then fill in or remove hair according to the outline.
No clinical studies or detailed reference material were found.
How it works: It acts only as a visual guide; the shape change comes from pencil, powder or hair removal.
Risks and caveats: No product-specific safety data were found. Shaping methods such as tweezing and waxing can be briefly painful, according to general references.
deepLead:
A brow shaping guide or stencil is a template placed over the eyebrow to outline a target shape, which the user then fills in with pencil or powder or uses as a boundary when trimming or removing stray hairs. Shaping is typically done by tweezing, waxing, threading or trimming.
No clinical studies of brow stencils were found, and the sources loaded for this article contain no product-specific information.

name: Brow growth serum

chain: Brow hairs look thicker or longer
angle.text: Users apply brow serums hoping for thicker, longer brows that frame the eyes better. Published evidence for the brow-thickening claim is limited to a safety test and one small trial without reported results.

summary: Cosmetic serums sold to thicken brows; published evidence is limited to a safety test and one small unreported trial.
note: Prostaglandin-containing products are drugs and regulated differently; growth data for cosmetic serums are lacking.
currentQuick:
Brow growth serums are topical cosmetics, often with peptides or plant extracts, marketed to make eyebrows look fuller. They are separate from prescription prostaglandin products such as bimatoprost.
Only limited research exists: one sponsored safety study of a lash and brow serum and one small registered trial without located results.
How it works: Cosmetic serums generally claim to condition hair or support growth through peptides and botanicals; no published study confirms a mechanism for brow growth.
Risks and caveats: Products near the eye can cause irritation or allergic reactions, which manufacturers screen with patch tests. Prostaglandin-based products have additional documented effects such as eye redness and skin darkening.
deepLead:
Brow growth serums are cosmetic products marketed to make eyebrows look thicker or longer. Many are peptide- or botanical-based; Wikipedia notes that some lash-growth brands use peptides rather than prostaglandins because of regulations in Canada and California.
Published evidence is sparse. A manufacturer-sponsored 2024 safety study tested a lash and brow serum for skin irritation rather than for growth, and a small registered trial of a brow serum is listed as completed, with no results located.

name: Vaseline on lashes/brows

angle.text: People dab petroleum jelly on lashes and brows as a cheap conditioner so the hairs look glossier and fuller. The sheen is visible right away; claims that it grows more hair are anecdotal and untested.

summary: Dabbing petroleum jelly on lashes and brows as a cheap conditioner; no studies show it grows hair.
note: Not a hair-growth treatment; keep product out of the eye.
currentQuick:
People apply petroleum jelly to lashes and brows to make them look glossier and fuller. It is a conditioning practice, not a recognized growth treatment.
No human studies found in the sources consulted have tested it for lash or brow growth.
How it works: Petroleum jelly forms an occlusive coating that reduces moisture loss and adds shine. It does not act on hair follicles.
Risks and caveats: Irritation if it gets in the eye is a general concern; some petroleum jelly products can contain trace hydrocarbons that regulators have commented on. Bimatoprost is the approved prescription lash product.
deepLead:
Applying petroleum jelly (Vaseline is the best-known brand) to eyelashes and eyebrows is a grooming practice promoted as a way to condition hair and make lashes or brows look fuller or glossier. Petroleum jelly is a semi-solid hydrocarbon mixture widely used in skin products to reduce moisture loss.
No published human studies found in the sources consulted have tested petroleum jelly for increasing lash or brow length or density. Wikipedia notes that lash length is largely set by genetics and that the only FDA-approved drug for lash growth is bimatoprost (Latisse, 2009), a prescription product.

name: Brow lift (surgical)

angle.text: Forum surgery packages include the brow lift to raise a low or heavy brow and open the eye area, and the change is visible once healed. The technique is well documented in plastic surgery literature; the claim that a higher brow is more attractive rests on opinion and limited rating studies.

summary: Surgery that raises a drooping brow and opens the eye area; well-documented in the plastic surgery literature, popular in forum surgery packages.
note: Surgical risks include numbness, hair loss at incisions, scarring and asymmetry.
currentQuick:
A surgical brow lift repositions the eyebrow and forehead tissue higher. It is used for drooping brows that crowd the eye and for forehead lines, and looksmaxxing forums treat it as part of eye-area hardmaxxing.
Techniques range from endoscopic and coronal lifts to direct and temporal lifts. Non-surgical options such as botulinum toxin and ultrasound devices are also studied.
How it works: The surgeon releases the brow tissue and fixes it in a higher position using incisions at the hairline, temple, brow or upper eyelid, depending on the technique.
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include numbness, hair loss, hairline elevation, scarring, asymmetry, infection and bleeding. Rates vary by technique and surgeon, and the literature describes serious complications as uncommon.
deepLead:
A surgical brow lift, also called a forehead lift, browlift or browplasty, is a cosmetic operation that raises a low or drooping eyebrow and softens horizontal forehead lines. It is also used when a heavy brow obstructs the upper visual field. Techniques include endoscopic, coronal, hairline (pretrichial), temporal, direct, mid-forehead and transblepharoplasty approaches.
In looksmaxxing communities it is classed as 'hardmaxxing' (surgical and procedural enhancement). Forum members discuss it mainly as part of the upper-third and eye-area toolkit, often alongside blepharoplasty, and often as one item in multi-procedure trips abroad. Proponents describe a higher brow position and a more open eye area as attractive; the published literature on brow lifts concerns aging, ptosis and patient satisfaction rather than attractiveness ideals in general.
Published research includes case series of endoscopic and direct brow lifts and studies of non-surgical alternatives such as botulinum toxin and energy-based devices. Complications are described in the literature as uncommon but include numbness, hair loss at incision sites, asymmetry and scarring, depending on technique.

name: Botox brow lift

angle.text: Users get small toxin injections to lift the outer brow without surgery, giving a visibly more open eye area for a few months. The lift has some trial data behind it and is temporary.

summary: Small toxin injections that let the brow tails sit higher without surgery; temporary, with some trial data behind it.
note: Brow or eyelid drooping and toxin spread are reported side effects; effects wear off.
currentQuick:
A botulinum toxin brow lift uses small injections to weaken muscles that pull the eyebrow down, letting the outer brow rest higher. It is discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a reversible alternative to surgical brow lifts.
The effect is temporary. A small case series and several registered Phase 4 trials have examined toxin for brow elevation.
How it works: Botulinum toxin type A relaxes the muscles it is injected into. Weakening brow depressors relative to the forehead muscle that lifts the brow can raise the brow position.
Risks and caveats: Reported side effects of cosmetic toxin include brow or eyelid drooping, bruising, headaches, spread of the toxin effect and, rarely, double vision. The FDA added boxed warnings about toxin spread in 2009. Botox Cosmetic is approved for glabellar lines; brow lifting is not a labeled use.
deepLead:
A botulinum toxin brow lift is a non-surgical technique in which small injections weaken muscles that pull the eyebrow down, letting the outer brow sit higher. Botox is the best-known brand; Dysport and others are also used.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to 'lift the tails' of the brows and open the eye area without surgery. Published research includes a 2000 case series on temporal brow elevation with botulinum toxin and several registered trials of toxin for brow position.
Effects are temporary. Wikipedia reports that cosmetic toxin effects typically last two to four months for glabellar lines, and brow or eyelid drooping is listed among reported side effects of some products.

name: Don't over-pluck / regrow

angle.text: Grooming advice says to stop tweezing so sparse brow areas can fill in and look fuller. Regrowth depends on whether follicles are still intact, and no trials test it.

summary: Stop plucking so brows can fill in; regrowth depends on whether follicles are intact, and no trials test it.
note: Permanent loss can occur if follicles are damaged; persistent loss warrants a clinician.
currentQuick:
This is the advice to stop tweezing brows to let them regrow. Tweezing is the most common shaping method.
Regrowth depends on whether the follicles are still intact. No clinical studies were found specific to over-plucking.
How it works: Plucking pulls the hair from the follicle. If follicles are not scarred, hair may regrow; if scarred, loss can be permanent.
Risks and caveats: Documented consequences of persistent pulling include permanent hair loss, and over-tweezed brows are a recognized reason for transplant surgery. Brow loss can also signal an underlying condition.
deepLead:
"Don't over-pluck" is advice in looksmaxxing and grooming circles to stop tweezing eyebrows so that sparse areas can fill in. Tweezing is the most common way to shape brows, and Wikipedia notes that plucked hairs can stop growing back over time, though that statement is flagged as needing a citation.
Hair loss from lashes and brows, called madarosis, depends on whether follicles survive: non-scarring loss may regrow when the cause is removed, while scarring loss is permanent and treated cosmetically, for example with transplantation. Wikipedia also notes that people who have over-tweezed are considered candidates for eyebrow transplants, and that constant pulling of lashes can cause permanent damage.

name: Eyebrow gel with fibers

angle.text: Users brush on fiber brow gel to make brows look thicker and fill gaps for the day. The fuller look is visible immediately and washes off; there is no clinical research on the product type.

summary: Brow gel with tiny fibers that fake fullness; a temporary cosmetic with no clinical research.
note: Cosmetic effect only; wears off.
currentQuick:
A brow gel with fibers sets hairs and adds tiny colored fibers that cling to fill gaps. It gives a temporary look of thicker brows.
No clinical studies were found for this product type.
How it works: The gel holds hairs in place while fibers adhere to hairs and skin to add visual density. It does not affect growth.
Risks and caveats: Eye-area irritation or allergy is possible with any cosmetic. Sources consulted give no product-specific safety data.
deepLead:
Eyebrow gel with fibers is a cosmetic that combines a brow-setting gel with tiny colored fibers that cling to hairs and skin to make brows look thicker or fill gaps. Wikipedia describes brow gels as adding texture and definition, and notes that powders, pencils and shaders are used to fill sparse areas; fibers specifically are not covered there.
No published clinical studies of fiber brow gels were found in the sources consulted. The product category is cosmetic and does not change hair growth.

name: Brow dyeing blonde / bleaching

angle.text: People bleach or dye brows lighter, often blonde, to soften the face or make a style statement. The colour change is visible right away; the chemistry is common hair bleaching, with no brow-specific research.

summary: Lightening brows with peroxide bleach or dye as a style choice; common chemistry, no brow-specific research.
note: Chemicals near the eye can irritate or cause allergic reactions.
currentQuick:
Brow bleaching lightens eyebrow hair, often to blonde, for a distinct look. Dyeing can instead darken brows.
No studies of brow bleaching were found in the sources consulted.
How it works: Hydrogen peroxide with an alkaline agent oxidizes melanin in the hair, lightening it. Dyes deposit color.
Risks and caveats: Irritation, allergic reactions (including to phenylenediamine dyes), breakage and discoloration are documented with hair coloring in general. The eye area is sensitive.
deepLead:
Bleaching or dyeing the eyebrows lighter, often blonde, is a style practice used to soften or alter the look of the brow. Hair bleaching works by oxidizing melanin with hydrogen peroxide in an alkaline mixture, with home products typically around 6% peroxide and salon products up to 12%, according to Wikipedia.
Wikipedia notes that hair coloring can cause skin irritation, allergy and hair breakage, and that phenylenediamine-based dyes can cause allergic reactions that may appear hours or a day later. The sources consulted contain no specific regulatory statements about bleaching eyebrows, and no published studies of brow bleaching were found.

name: Brow slitting / cuts

angle.text: Users shave one or more thin slits through the eyebrow as a streetwear-style statement that is visible at once and grows back. It is a styling choice and has barely been studied.

summary: A shaved gap cut through the eyebrow as a style statement; temporary, cosmetic, and barely studied.
note: No published research on the style; the main practical limit is that the hair regrows.
currentQuick:
Brow slitting is a grooming style where a thin line of hair is shaved out of the eyebrow. It has been popular with some young people since at least the 1990s and is a fashion choice rather than a structural change.
Sources on the style are thin. Encyclopedias mention it only briefly, and no studies have tested its effect on how a face is perceived.
How it works: Hair is trimmed or shaved from a narrow strip of the brow with a razor or trimmer, leaving bare skin visible. Nothing is done to the skin or follicle, so the gap grows back.
Risks and caveats: Shaving carries the usual minor risks of razor use such as nicks or irritation. A 2008 news report cited by Wikipedia linked the style to gang concerns in some schools, which can matter where school or workplace dress rules apply.
deepLead:
Brow slitting, also called eyebrow slits or brow cuts, is a grooming style in which one or more thin lines are shaved or cut through the eyebrow hair so that bare skin shows in a short vertical or diagonal gap. It is purely a hair-styling choice and is usually done with a razor or trimmer; it does not involve cutting skin.
Wikipedia's general article on eyebrows notes that shaving lines into the eyebrows was popular among some younger people in the 1990s and 2000s, and cites a 2008 news report that linked the trend to gang concerns in schools . Beyond that mention, little encyclopedic or scientific material exists on the style itself, so this article is short.

name: Unibrow trimming / bridge shaping

chain: Brows read as two clean arcs
angle.text: Users pluck, wax, thread or shave the bridge between the brows so they look separate and the glabella looks clean. The result is visible immediately and reversible, and whether a unibrow counts as a flaw varies by culture.

summary: Removing or shaping the hair bridging the brows; cheap and reversible, with culture deciding whether it counts as a flaw.
note: No studies test its effect on attractiveness; permanent removal options carry their own risks.
currentQuick:
A unibrow (synophrys) is hair connecting the eyebrows over the nose bridge. Trimming or shaping it means removing that hair so the brows look separate, using tweezers, wax, thread, a razor or longer-lasting methods.
It is a common, usually harmless polygenic trait. Views differ by culture: some historical and modern societies admire joined brows while many Western settings do not.
How it works: Hair across the glabella is plucked, waxed, threaded, shaved or trimmed. Plucking and waxing pull hair from the root and it regrows over weeks; laser and electrolysis aim at the follicle for longer-lasting reduction.
Risks and caveats: Grooming can cause temporary redness, pain or ingrown hairs. Rarely, synophrys is one feature of a genetic syndrome, which is a medical rather than cosmetic matter. No studies have tested how bridge shaping changes perceived attractiveness.
deepLead:
A unibrow, medically called synophrys, is hair that joins the two eyebrows across the glabella, the smooth area above the bridge of the nose. Unibrow trimming or bridge shaping is the grooming practice of removing or thinning that hair, by plucking, waxing, threading, shaving, or in some cases permanent hair-removal methods, so that the brows appear separate, or of deliberately keeping or shaping the bridge .
Synophrys is common in the general population and is usually a benign, polygenic trait, although it can also be one of several facial features in some rare genetic syndromes . Cultural views of the trait vary: connected brows have been prized in some historical and contemporary settings and disfavoured in others .

name: Eflornithine (Vaniqa)

angle.text: Women use this prescription cream to slow facial hair regrowth so less shaving or plucking is needed. It is approved for that purpose and its effect lasts only while it is used; it is not hair removal.

summary: Prescription cream that slows facial hair regrowth in women; it works only while used and is not hair removal.
note: Hair returns to its prior rate within about 8 weeks of stopping; acne is the most reported side effect.
currentQuick:
Eflornithine cream (Vaniqa, 13.9 percent) is an FDA-approved prescription treatment for unwanted facial hair in women. It is used together with shaving, plucking or light-based hair reduction rather than instead of them.
In the two vehicle-controlled trials behind its approval, more women improved on the cream than on vehicle, although many showed only partial improvement and regrowth returned after stopping.
How it works: It irreversibly inhibits ornithine decarboxylase, an enzyme needed for polyamine production and cell growth, which slows the growth of new hair in follicles. It does not destroy follicles.
Risks and caveats: The most common reported effect is acne, followed by local irritation such as stinging, redness, dryness and itching. It is prescription-only in the US and generally elsewhere. Limited pregnancy data show no clear harm, but interaction studies are lacking.
deepLead:
Eflornithine, also known as difluoromethylornithine (DFMO), is an inhibitor of the enzyme ornithine decarboxylase. Its 13.9 percent topical cream, sold as Vaniqa, is a prescription product approved in the United States in December 2000 to reduce unwanted facial hair in women . Systemic forms of the same molecule are used for other conditions, including second-stage African sleeping sickness and, since 2023, maintenance therapy in high-risk neuroblastoma .
Topical eflornithine does not remove hair. Reports describe it as slowing regrowth, with hair returning to its previous rate within about eight weeks of stopping . In looksmaxxing and grooming contexts it is mainly relevant to facial and beard-area hair reduction, usually alongside shaving, laser or electrolysis.
